title: Part 2, Chapter 69
paragraphs: Concerning the strangest and most extraordinary adventure that happened to Don Quixote in the entire course of this great history

The horsemen dismounted, and together with the men on foot they lifted Sancho and Don Quixote bodily, without a moment's pause, and carried them into the courtyard. Around its whole perimeter nearly a hundred torches burned in their sockets, with more than five hundred lamps along the corridors besides, so that although the night was fairly dark, no one could have missed the daylight. In the middle of the courtyard stood a catafalque, raised about two yards off the ground and draped entirely in an enormous canopy of black velvet, and on the steps surrounding it white wax tapers burned in more than a hundred silver candlesticks. On the catafalque lay the dead body of a young woman so lovely that her beauty made death itself look beautiful. Her head rested on a brocade cushion and was crowned with a garland of fragrant flowers of many kinds; her hands were crossed on her breast, and between them lay a branch of yellow victory palm. On one side of the courtyard a stage had been erected, where two figures sat on two chairs; the crowns on their heads and the scepters in their hands suggested they were kings of some description, whether genuine or theatrical. Beside this stage, which was reached by a flight of steps, stood two more chairs, and on these the men carrying the prisoners seated Don Quixote and Sancho, all in complete silence, indicating by gestures that they too were to keep quiet—though they would have done so without any prompting, since astonishment at everything they were seeing had left them speechless. Now two persons of obvious rank, whom Don Quixote immediately recognized as his hosts the duke and duchess, climbed onto the stage with a large retinue and took their places on two magnificent chairs beside the two apparent kings. Who would not have been astounded by all this? And that was not the whole of it, for Don Quixote had realized that the dead body on the catafalque was that of the beautiful Altisidora. As the duke and duchess mounted the stage, Don Quixote and Sancho rose and bowed deeply to them, and they answered with a slight inclination of their heads. At that moment an official crossed the courtyard, came up to Sancho, and threw over him a robe of black buckram painted all over with flames of fire; then, removing his cap, he set on his head a mitre of the kind worn by those sentenced by the Holy Office, whispering in his ear that he must not open his mouth or they would gag him, or kill him. Sancho looked himself over from head to foot and saw that he was blazing with flames; but since they did not burn him, he did not care two farthings about them. He took off the mitre, saw that it was painted with devils, and put it back on, saying to himself, "Well, so far the flames aren't burning me and the devils aren't carrying me off." Don Quixote looked him over as well, and although fear had overwhelmed his senses, he could not help smiling at the figure Sancho cut. And now, from beneath the catafalque it seemed, there rose a low, sweet sound of flutes which, unbroken by any human voice—for there silence itself kept silence—had a soft and melting effect. Then, suddenly, beside the pillow of what appeared to be the corpse, a handsome youth dressed in the Roman style appeared, and to the accompaniment of a harp that he played himself, he sang these two stanzas in a sweet, clear voice:

While fair Altisidora, made the toy
of cold Don Quixote's unfeeling cruelty,
returns to life, and in this enchanted court
the ladies dress in sables for the scene,
and while her matrons, all in proper form,
robe my lady in baize and bombazine,
I will sing her beauty and her sorrows here
with a defter quill than ever struck the Thracian string.

But it is not in life alone, I think,
that this office falls to me; Lady, when my tongue
lies cold in death, believe me, even then
my voice will raise its tribute song to you.
My soul, set free from this cramped prison-house,
drifting along across the Stygian lake,
will go its way still singing in your praise,
and make the waters of oblivion stand still.

At this point one of the two who looked like kings called out, "Enough, enough, divine singer! It would take forever to recount for us now the death and the charms of the peerless Altisidora—who is not dead, as the ignorant world supposes, but alive in the voice of fame and in the penance that Sancho Panza, here present, must undergo to restore her to the light she has lost. Therefore, O Rhadamanthus, you who sit in judgment with me in the murky caverns of Dis, since you know everything the inscrutable fates have decreed concerning the revival of this damsel, announce and declare it at once, so that the happiness we expect from her restoration is delayed no longer."
Scarcely had Minos, Rhadamanthus's fellow judge, finished saying this when Rhadamanthus stood up and declared:

"Ho, officials of this house, high and low, great and small, hurry here every one of you, and plant twenty-four smacks on Sancho's face, and give him twelve pinches and six pin-pricks in the back and arms; for on this ceremony depends the restoration of Altisidora."

When Sancho heard this he broke his silence and cried out, "By all that's holy, I'll let my face be smacked and pawed at the day I turn Moor. Body of me! What does manhandling my face have to do with this damsel's resurrection? 'The old woman took kindly to the blits.' They enchant Dulcinea, and I get whipped to disenchant her; Altisidora dies of whatever ailments God chose to send her, and to bring her back to life I have to take twenty-four smacks, have my body punctured with pins, and have my arms pinched until they're covered in welts! Try those jokes on a brother-in-law; 'I'm an old dog, and tus, tus doesn't work on me.'"

"You shall die," said Rhadamanthus in a loud voice. "Relent, you tiger; humble yourself, proud Nimrod; suffer and be silent, for nothing impossible is being asked of you, and it is not your place to question the difficulties of this matter. Smacked you must be, pricked you shall find yourself, and pinched until you howl. Come, officials, I say, carry out my orders—or, on the word of an honest man, you will see what you were born for."

At this, some six duennas appeared, advancing across the courtyard in procession one behind the other, four of them wearing spectacles, and all with their right hands raised, showing four fingers' width of wrist to make their hands look longer, as the fashion now dictates. The moment Sancho caught sight of them he bellowed like a bull and shouted, "I might let the whole world handle me, but let duennas touch me—never! Scratch my face, the way my master was treated in this very castle; run me through the body with polished daggers; pinch my arms with red-hot pincers—I'll bear it all patiently to oblige these noble people. But I won't let duennas lay a finger on me, even if the devil carries me off!"

Here Don Quixote broke his silence too, saying to Sancho, "Be patient, my son, and oblige these noble persons, and give heaven all your thanks for having placed such virtue in your person that through its sufferings you can disenchant the enchanted and bring the dead back to life."

By now the duennas were close upon Sancho, and he, grown more docile and reasonable, settled himself properly in his chair and offered his face and beard to the first of them, who delivered a very firmly planted smack and then dropped him a low curtsey.
"Less courtesy and less face-paint, señora duenna," said Sancho; "by God, your hands smell of vinegar-wash."

One after another, all the duennas smacked him, and several other members of the household pinched him; but what he could not endure was the pricking of the pins. So, his patience apparently exhausted, he sprang up from his chair, seized a lighted torch standing nearby, and went after the duennas and the whole crew of his tormentors, shouting, "Away with you, ministers of hell! I'm not made of brass, that I should feel nothing under such outlandish tortures."

At that instant Altisidora—who was probably tired of lying on her back for so long—turned onto her side, and at the sight of it the onlookers cried out almost in one voice, "Altisidora is alive! Altisidora lives!"

Rhadamanthus ordered Sancho to lay aside his anger, since the purpose they had been pursuing was now achieved. The moment Don Quixote saw Altisidora stir, he dropped to his knees before Sancho and said to him, "Now is the moment, son of my heart—not merely my squire—for you to give yourself some of those lashes you are bound to administer for the disenchantment of Dulcinea. Now, I say, is the time when the virtue within you is ripe and charged with power to work the good that is expected of you."

To which Sancho replied, "That's trick piled on trick, if you ask me, and not honey on pancakes. A fine thing it would be to get a whipping now, on top of pinches, smacks, and pin-jabbings! You might as well tie a big stone around my neck and throw me down a well—I'd hardly mind, if I'm forever to be made the wedding-cow that pays for curing other people's ailments. Leave me alone, or by God I'll throw the whole business to the dogs, come what may."

By this time Altisidora had sat up on the catafalque, and as she did, the clarions rang out, joined by the flutes and by the voices of everyone present crying, "Long live Altisidora! Long live Altisidora!" The duke and duchess and the kings Minos and Rhadamanthus rose to their feet, and all of them, together with Don Quixote and Sancho, went forward to receive her and help her down from the catafalque. She, acting as though she were just coming out of a faint, bowed her head to the duke and duchess and to the kings, and glancing sideways at Don Quixote, said to him, "God forgive you, unfeeling knight, for thanks to your cruelty I have spent what feels to me like more than a thousand years in the other world; and to you, the most compassionate man on earth, I give thanks for the life I now enjoy. From this day forward, friend Sancho, count as yours six smocks of mine, which I give you to make into as many shirts for yourself; and if they are not all entirely whole, at least they are all clean."

Sancho kissed her hands in gratitude, kneeling, with the mitre in his hand. The duke ordered it taken from him, his cap and doublet returned, and the flaming robe removed. Sancho begged the duke to let him keep the robe and mitre, since he wanted to carry them home as a token and keepsake of that unparalleled adventure. The duchess said they must indeed be left with him, for he already knew what a great friend of his she was. The duke then gave orders for the courtyard to be cleared, for everyone to withdraw to their rooms, and for Don Quixote and Sancho to be escorted back to their old quarters.
